The results speak to that assumption in two ways. `r iff(!emp_up && !lfp_up, "First, a co-resident grandmother is not associated with more paid work by mothers, so family care does not substitute for formal childcare in its labour-market effect, even where it is available. Expanding formal childcare may matter for mothers in extended households as well as in nuclear ones, although its effect will depend on whether the constraints of the extended household also bind on the use of formal care.", "First, a co-resident grandmother is associated with more paid work by mothers, which suggests that the scarcity of formal childcare is most binding for the mothers in nuclear households who lack this support.")` `r iff(gm_cost_cc, "Second, family care is not free: it is provided by older women whose own time responds to the presence of a young grandchild. As India's population ages [@unfpa2023ageing; @iips2020lasi], the supply of grandmother care will compete with the older generation's own work and care needs, and its implicit cost belongs in any assessment of public childcare.", "Second, the care that grandmothers provide does not respond strongly to the presence of a young grandchild in these data, which limits how far policy can count on it.")`

## Limitations

The limitations are those of a single cross-section of diaries. Living arrangements are chosen, and the comparisons across arrangement types, the gradients by grandparent type, the placebo and the coefficient-stability bounds narrow but do not eliminate the scope for selection. Candidate instruments used elsewhere, such as the survival of grandparents or the husband's birth order, are not available in the survey. One diary day per person measures a day, not a routine [@frazis2012think], which adds noise to individual outcomes but does not bias population means. Children under six are counted as a residual from household size and are assigned to a mother by a generational rule; I show that the main estimate is robust to restricting to households where the assignment is unambiguous, but misassignment in households with several junior couples cannot be ruled out. The roster code for parents of the head does not distinguish the head's own parents from the spouse's parents, so for head-level mothers I cannot separate the maternal from the paternal grandmother. Grandmother age proxies for health only imperfectly. Finally, the survey does not record which child a care episode is for. In households with several young children, or with children of more than one couple, the grandmother's recorded care may serve children other than the mother's. Future rounds that record the recipient of care, and household surveys that follow the same families over the birth of a grandchild, would allow sharper tests.

# Conclusion {#conclusion}

Diaries for every member of the household allow a direct test of an assumption that runs through discussion of the care economy in India: that co-resident grandmothers lighten the load of mothers of young children. Identifying the generation above each mother correctly matters for the test, because in patrilocal households the young mother lives in her parents-in-law's household and, without care, the head's wife would be counted as a mother rather than as the grandmother she is. `r iff(sub_child && !emp_up && !lfp_up, "With that identification, co-resident grandmothers are associated with less childcare by mothers, but not with more paid work.", iff(sub_child && (emp_up || lfp_up), "With that identification, co-resident grandmothers are associated with less childcare by mothers and with more paid work.", iff(!sub_child && !emp_up && !lfp_up, "With that identification, co-resident grandmothers are not associated with less childcare by mothers or with more paid work by them.", "With that identification, co-resident grandmothers are associated with more paid work by mothers but not with less childcare.")))` `r iff(gm_cost_cc, paste0("Grandmothers themselves provide ", pct(gm_share_cc, 0), " of the combined childcare of the two women, and their own childcare is higher when a young grandchild is present."), "")` Family care in India is therefore best understood not as a free substitute for formal childcare, but as a transfer of time between women of two generations whose terms are set by the structure of the household.
